title: Additive-Character Dependence of the Quadratic Gauss Sum
description: The parent entry proves the square identity $g^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}p = p^*$ for the quadratic Gauss sum $g = \operatorname{gaussSum}(\chi, \psi)$ of an odd prime $p$ and a primitive additive character $\psi : \mathbb{Z}/p \to \mathbb{C}$. This entry determines the dependence of $g$ on the choice of $\psi$. Every other primitive additive character has the form $\operatorname{mulShift}\psi\,a$ for a unit $a$, and Mathlib's twisting law combined with the fact that the quadratic character takes values $\pm 1$ on units gives the clean formula $\operatorname{gaussSum}(\chi, \operatorname{mulShift}\psi\,a) = \chi(a)\,g$ (`gaussSum_chiC_mulShift`). Three structural consequences follow: the square is twist-independent, so $g^2 = p^*$ is intrinsic to $p$ (`gaussSum_chiC_mulShift_sq_eq`); $g$ is nonzero for every primitive $\psi$ (`gaussSum_chiC_ne_zero`); and the twist fixes $g$ exactly when $a$ is a quadratic residue (`gaussSum_mulShift_eq_self_iff`) and negates it exactly when $a$ is a non-residue (`gaussSum_mulShift_eq_neg_iff`). In words: replacing the additive character $\psi$ by $\operatorname{mulShift}\psi\,a$ flips the sign of the quadratic Gauss sum precisely on the non-residues and leaves the square untouched. The square identity is re-derived in-file from Mathlib's generic `gaussSum_sq`, so the file imports only `Mathlib`. Fully machine-verified with no sorries and no axioms beyond Lean's foundational three.
overview: {"historicalContext": "Gauss introduced the sum $g = \\sum_{n} \\chi(n)\\,\\psi(n)$ — with $\\chi$ the quadratic character and $\\psi$ an additive character of $\\mathbb{Z}/p$ — in his work on biquadratic reciprocity and the constructibility of regular polygons. The *square* $g^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}p = p^*$ is the elementary algebraic kernel of the theory (the parent entry). But $g$ itself manifestly depends on the choice of additive character $\\psi$: a different primitive $\\psi$ generally gives a different value. Determining exactly how $g$ varies with $\\psi$ — the orbit of $g$ under the $(p-1)$ primitive characters — is the natural structural question, and it is precisely what makes $g^2$ (and hence $p^*$) a well-defined invariant of $p$ alone.", "problemStatement": "Fix an odd prime $p$, let $\\chi = \\mathrm{chiC}\\,p : \\mathbb{Z}/p \\to \\mathbb{C}$ be the quadratic character and $\\psi$ a primitive additive character, with $g = \\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi,\\psi)$. Every other primitive additive character is $\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a$ for a unit $a$. Determine $\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi, \\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a)$ in terms of $g$, decide for which $a$ the twist fixes resp. negates $g$, and show the square $g^2 = p^*$ is independent of the chosen additive character.", "proofStrategy": "The engine is Mathlib's twisting law `gaussSum_mulShift`: $\\chi(a)\\cdot\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi,\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a) = \\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi,\\psi)$. Because $\\chi$ is a *quadratic* character, its value on any unit is $\\pm 1$ (`chiC_unit_cases`, from the trichotomy of `IsQuadratic` plus nonvanishing $\\chi(a)\\chi(a^{-1}) = \\chi(1) = 1$), hence $\\chi(a)^2 = 1$. Multiplying the twisting law through by the involution $\\chi(a)$ rearranges it to the clean form $\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi,\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a) = \\chi(a)\\cdot g$ (`gaussSum_chiC_mulShift`). Squaring kills the $\\pm 1$ factor, so every twist has the same square $p^*$ (`gaussSum_chiC_mulShift_sq_eq`), re-derived in-file from `gaussSum_sq`. For the fixed/negated dichotomy, nonvanishing of $g$ (`gaussSum_chiC_ne_zero`, via `gaussSum_ne_zero_of_nontrivial`) lets one cancel $g$ from $\\chi(a)\\,g = \\pm g$, reducing to $\\chi(a) = \\pm 1$; the bridges `chiC_eq_one_iff` / `chiC_eq_neg_one_iff` and `quadraticChar_one_iff_isSquare` / `quadraticChar_neg_one_iff_not_isSquare` translate these into `IsSquare a` resp. `¬ IsSquare a`.", "keyInsights": ["The Gauss sum $g$ genuinely depends on the additive character $\\psi$, but only by the sign $\\chi(a) = \\pm 1$ when $\\psi$ is replaced by $\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a$. This is the exact mechanism by which the *square* $g^2 = p^*$ becomes a character-independent invariant of $p$: squaring annihilates the only freedom, the $\\pm 1$.", "Twisting the additive character by $a$ flips the sign of $g$ precisely when $a$ is a quadratic non-residue mod $p$, and fixes $g$ precisely when $a$ is a residue. The arithmetic of $\\mathbb{Z}/p$ (residue vs non-residue) is thus read off directly from the analytic transformation behaviour of the Gauss sum.", "The clean twisting form $\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi,\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a) = \\chi(a)\\,g$ is obtained from Mathlib's $\\chi(a)\\,\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi,\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a) = g$ by multiplying through by $\\chi(a)$ and using $\\chi(a)^2 = 1$ — turning a relation that hides $g$ behind a factor into an explicit formula for the twist, with no case split needed in the algebra.", "Nonvanishing $g \\neq 0$ is what upgrades the value computation to an `iff`: without it, $\\chi(a)\\,g = g$ would not force $\\chi(a) = 1$. It comes for free from `gaussSum_ne_zero_of_nontrivial` since $(p : \\mathbb{C}) \\neq 0$ and $\\chi$ is nontrivial."]}
conclusion: {"summary": "For an odd prime $p$ and primitive additive character $\\psi$, the quadratic Gauss sum $g = \\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\mathrm{chiC}\\,p, \\psi)$ transforms under a twist of the additive character by the simple law $\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi, \\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a) = \\chi(a)\\,g$. Consequently $g$ is nonzero, its square $g^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$ is independent of the chosen additive character, the twist fixes $g$ exactly when $a$ is a quadratic residue, and negates $g$ exactly when $a$ is a non-residue. All five statements are machine-verified with no sorries and no axioms beyond Lean's foundational three.", "implications": "This pins down the additive-character dependence of the quadratic Gauss sum completely and explains, at the most elementary level, why the parent entry's value $p^* = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$ is a well-defined invariant of $p$ rather than an artefact of a particular $\\psi$: the $(p-1)$ primitive characters split $g$ into just two values $\\pm g$, distinguished by the residue/non-residue dichotomy, and squaring erases the distinction. The residue $\\leftrightarrow$ sign correspondence is the same Legendre-symbol bookkeeping that drives the Gauss-sum proof of quadratic reciprocity, here isolated as a transformation law.", "openQuestions": ["The two primitive characters $\\psi$ and $\\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a$ with $a$ a non-residue give $g$ and $-g$; can one formalise the orbit count — that the $(p-1)$ primitive additive characters yield exactly the two values $\\{+g, -g\\}$, each attained $(p-1)/2$ times — as a clean group action of $(\\mathbb{Z}/p)^\\times$ on the Gauss sums?", "Does the same twisting law $\\operatorname{gaussSum}(\\chi, \\operatorname{mulShift}\\psi\\,a) = \\chi(a)\\,g$ extend verbatim to higher-order (e.g. cubic or quartic) characters, where $\\chi(a)$ is a genuine root of unity rather than $\\pm 1$, and what replaces the residue/non-residue dichotomy there?"]}

crossReferences.description: The parent establishes the square identity $g^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}p$. This entry explains why that value is well-defined independent of the additive character $\psi$: every twist of $\psi$ scales $g$ by $\pm 1$, so the square is intrinsic to $p$.

The sibling oq-01 extracts the real/imaginary dichotomy and magnitude $\|g\|^2 = p$ from the square identity. This entry is the orthogonal structural axis: how $g$ varies with the additive character rather than how it sits in $\mathbb{C}$.

The sibling oq-02 proves the equidistribution of residues and non-residues ($\sum_a \chi(a) = 0$). The residue/non-residue dichotomy reappears here as the criterion deciding whether a twist of the additive character fixes or negates the Gauss sum.
